title: Incident: Amazon S3 disruption, February 2017
objective: Follow AWS's summary of the February 2017 S3 disruption: how one mistyped input removed too many servers, why restarting took hours, and what AWS changed.

sources.title: AWS: Summary of the Amazon S3 Service Disruption in the Northern Virginia (US-EAST-1) Region: "one of the inputs to the command was entered incorrectly and a larger set of servers was removed than intended"

simplifies: Simplified to its key moments from AWS's own summary (times are PST, as AWS gives them). The summary's detail about which request types recovered when is shortened.

steps.caption: An authorised S3 engineer, following an established playbook, ran a command to remove a small number of servers. "One of the inputs to the command was entered incorrectly and a larger set of servers was removed than intended."

The removed servers supported the index subsystem, which "manages the metadata and location information of all S3 objects in the region", and the placement subsystem. Both needed a full restart, and while they restarted, S3 was unable to service requests.

predict.prompt: Those servers supported two other S3 subsystems. Too much of their capacity is suddenly gone. What happens?

options.explanation: Too much capacity went at once to just slow down.

options.text: Nothing: S3 keeps spare servers for this
options.explanation: AWS's summary says each needed a full restart.

options.text: Both subsystems need a full restart, and S3 can't serve requests while they restart
options.explanation: Right. Removing that much capacity at once meant restarting them from scratch.

steps.caption: The restarts were slow: "we have not completely restarted the index subsystem or the placement subsystem in our larger regions for many years", and S3 had grown massively since then.

predict.prompt: Why would a restart that once took minutes now take hours?

options.text: The system had grown enormously since anyone last did a full restart, so the restart had never been tried at this size
options.explanation: Right. A recovery path you never exercise can quietly get slower as you grow.
The steps were known; the scale was new.
It's about size: the same restart on a much bigger system.

steps.caption: AWS's status dashboard couldn't show the problem: AWS "were unable to update the individual services' status on the AWS Service Health Dashboard", so it posted updates on its Twitter account and as banner text instead.
"By 12:26PM PST, the index subsystem had activated enough capacity to begin servicing S3 GET, LIST, and DELETE requests."
"By 1:18PM PST, the index subsystem was fully recovered", and S3 "finished recovery at 1:54PM PST."

What AWS changed: the tool "allowed too much capacity to be removed too quickly", so it now removes capacity more slowly, with safeguards against going below a minimum; and S3 is being split into smaller partitions called cells, so a restart is smaller.

quiz.prompt: What was the root problem with the tool, according to AWS?

options.text: It was used by the wrong person
options.explanation: AWS says the engineer was authorised and following a playbook.

options.text: It let too much capacity be removed too quickly, so one typo could do huge damage
options.explanation: Right. The fix limits how much and how fast it can remove.
AWS's fix was about limits, not undo.

quiz.prompt: Why does splitting a service into cells help?

options.explanation: The goal is limiting damage, not speed.

options.text: Each cell is smaller, so a mistake or a restart affects less and finishes sooner
options.explanation: Right. Smaller pieces mean a smaller blast radius.

options.text: Cells stop people from making typos
options.explanation: Typos still happen; cells limit how far they reach.
